title: Why don’t time zones follow straight lines?

sources.name: IANA — Time-zone database and civil-time changes
Royal Museums Greenwich — Local time and the railways

practice: Explore the places behind the clock changes with World Capitals.

sections.html:
As Earth rotates, different places face the Sun at different times. Divide a full rotation of 360 degrees by 24 hours and you get 15 degrees per hour. It seems natural to divide the world into neat strips.

Actual time-zone boundaries are less tidy. Governments choose civil time to suit borders and daily life, so the lines bend around countries and regions rather than following longitude exactly.
sections.title: The idea behind time zones

sections.html:
A UTC offset tells you how far a local clock is ahead of or behind UTC at a particular moment. A time zone includes the rules that determine that offset, including any daylight-saving changes.

Two places may change their clocks on different dates, or one may not change them at all. The difference between them can therefore vary during the year.

For a call or a journey, check the cities and the date in a calendar or time-zone tool. IANA’s time-zone database is updated as governments change the rules.
sections.title: Why the time difference can change

sections.html:
Suppose City A is at UTC+2 and City B is at UTC−3. When it is 14:00 in A, subtract two hours to get 12:00 UTC. Subtract three more to find the time in B: 09:00.

Going through UTC gives you a clear intermediate step. Around midnight, remember to check the date as well.

It is 01:00 on Tuesday at UTC+2. What time is it at UTC−3?

20:00 on Monday. Subtracting two hours gives 23:00 Monday UTC, then subtracting three more gives 20:00.

sections.html: The example above supplies fixed offsets, so it is a straightforward calculation. For a real city, you first need to know which offset applies on that date. Longitude alone cannot tell you its current legal time.

description: Earth’s rotation gives us a starting point, but borders and daylight-saving rules make local time more complicated.

questions.prompt: What does a UTC offset tell you?
options: A clock’s difference from UTC at a given time
questions.explanation: An offset gives a difference at a particular moment. A time zone also includes the rules that can change that offset.

questions.prompt: It is 14:00 at UTC+2. What time is it at UTC−3, using those fixed offsets?
questions.explanation: Subtract two hours to get 12:00 UTC, then subtract three more: 09:00.

questions.prompt: Why should a real international meeting include both city and date?
options: Time-zone rules can change the applicable offset
Longitude always gives the legal time
All places change their clocks together
questions.explanation: The place and date determine the applicable civil-time rules, including daylight saving where used.
